body: ### What would you like to be added? Following the proposal to introduce Resource Size as a new Scalability Dimension ([#134375](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375)), I would like to propose establishing "Pod Shape" as its own formal scalability envelope. We should clearly separate the concepts of: * **Shape:** Which fields are set and their proportions (e.g., number of init containers, sidecars, volumes). * **Size:** The size of the field values themselves, which can be adjusted independently. The goal is to align as a community on an "Exemplar Pod Shape" that we guarantee to be scalable. Once aligned, we should formally document this shape envelope in the community configurations and limits ([thresholds.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md)). ### Why is this needed? While addressing resource size limits is crucial, [recent analyses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375#issuecomment-3952087283) have shown that the types of fields set in a Pod spec can have a disproportionate, non-linear impact on resulting Pod size and control plane load. Currently, our tests generate a specific total size in etcd by using a "flat" pod shape and stuffing a large random payload into a single environment variable. However, real-world users achieve the same overall pod size by utilizing complex architectural patterns (like sidecars and init containers), which generate drastically different cascading overheads: * **Names & ManagedFields:** Labels, annotations, and the names of containers, environment variables or fields are recorded by the API server as object metadata to track controller field ownership. In practice, this often leads to a **doubling of the Pod size**. * **Init Containers or Readiness Gates:** Each forces Kubelet to send two additional status updates. Adding just one init container or readiness gate **increases scheduling cycle writes by 50%** (from 4 to 6), inflating watch events and watch cache memory for all controllers. * **Container** - Each init or sidecar container requires an individual status tracking, adding roughly **1KB of overhead** via image digests and sandbox metadata. # Current Test Shape vs. Intended Exemplar Shape To illustrate the gap, here is a comparison between the current test pod shape and the intended exemplar pod shape. Both have a total pod size in etcd of roughly 10KB, but achieve it in completely different ways: | Field | Current Test Pod Shape | Proposed Exemplar Pod Shape | | --------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | | Annotations | 0 | 10 | | Labels | 1 | 10 | | Init Containers | 0 | 2 | | Containers | 1 | 2 | | Volumes | 2 | 10 per container/init container | | Envs | 1 | 10 per container/init container | | Env Value | 6KB | Minimal to hit intended pod size| | Total Pod Size (etcd) | ~10KB | ~10KB | ## Proposed Plan 1. **Align on the Exemplar Pod Shape:** Finalize the proposed shape outlined above as the target baseline envelope to ensure realistic size overhead and API usage. 2. **Update Scalability tests and Benchmarks** Update K8s scalability tests and benchmarks to reflect exemplar pod. 3. **Fuzzing & Investigation:** Conduct fuzzing on other pod fields to identify any remaining areas with non-linear performance impacts. 2. **Document** Add this defined shape envelope to [sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md) to formally guarantee its scalability. ## Tracking Before vs After | | Before | After (Still in progress) | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------- | | Pod Size | 10.15 KB | 10.29 KB (+1.4%) | | Pod Resource Size | 1571 MB | 1601 MB (+2%) | | Number of Writes in Scheduling Cycle | 4 | 8 | | Managed Fields Overhead | 20.6% | 48.80% | | [API Server Memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-apiserver-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-apiserver&Resource=memory) | 53.6 GB | 61 GB (+14%) | | [API Server CPU](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-apiserver-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-apiserver&Resource=cpu) | 38 cores | 47.5 (+25%) | | [KCM Memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-controller-manager-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-controller-manager&Resource=memory) | 9.3 GB | 11.9 GB (+28%) | | [Scheduler Memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-scheduler-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-scheduler&Resource=memory) | 7.6 GB | 10.0 GB (+31.6%) | | [Etcd events memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=etcd-manager-events-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fetcd-manager&Resource=memory) | 2.3GB | 3.3GB (+43%) | | Pod Shape | | | /sig scalability /sig api-machinery /cc @wojtek-t @mborsz @liggitt

In response to [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415):

>### What would you like to be added?
>
>Following the proposal to introduce Resource Size as a new Scalability Dimension ([#134375](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375)), I would like to propose establishing "Pod Shape" as its own formal scalability envelope.
>
>We should clearly separate the concepts of:
>
>* **Shape:** Which fields are set and their proportions (e.g., number of init containers, sidecars, volumes).
>* **Size:** The size of the field values themselves, which can be adjusted independently.
>
>The goal is to align as a community on an "Exemplar Pod Shape" that we guarantee to be scalable. Once aligned, we should formally document this shape envelope in the community configurations and limits ([thresholds.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md)).
>
>### Why is this needed?
>
>While addressing resource size limits is crucial, [recent analyses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375#issuecomment-3952087283) have shown that the types of fields set in a Pod spec can have a disproportionate, non-linear impact on resulting Pod size and control plane load. 
>
>Currently, our tests generate a specific total size in etcd by using a "flat" pod shape and stuffing a large random payload into a single environment variable. However, real-world users achieve the same overall pod size by utilizing complex architectural patterns (like sidecars and init containers), which generate drastically different cascading overheads:
>* **ManagedFields:** These are automatically generated to track field ownership and [often double the size](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/555-server-side-apply#scalability) of the entire pod specification. It's size depends on number of fields set which is not tested at all. 
>* **Init Containers:** Adding just one init container causes the Kubelet to send two additional status updates. This increases the number of writes in a standard pod scheduling cycle by 50% (from 4 to 6 writes), generating significantly more watch events for all controllers and inflating watch cache memory.
>* **Sidecars:** Each sidecar container requires its own container status entry, which adds approximately 1KB of overhead due to image digests and sandbox metadata.
>
># Current Test Shape vs. Intended Exemplar Shape
>
>To illustrate the gap, here is a comparison between the current test pod shape and the intended exemplar pod shape. Both have a total pod size in etcd of roughly 10KB, but achieve it in completely different ways:
>
>| Field                 | Current Test Pod Shape | Proposed Exemplar Pod Shape     |
>| --------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- |
>| Annotations           | 0                      | 10                              |
>| Labels                | 1                      | 10                              |
>| Init Containers       | 0                      | 2                               |
>| Containers            | 1                      | 2                               |
>| Volumes               | 2                      | 10 per container/init container                             |
>| Envs                  | 1                      | 10 per container/init container |
>| Env Value             | 6KB                    | Minimal to hit intended pod size|
>| Total Pod Size (etcd) | ~10KB                  | ~10KB                           |
>
>## Proposed Plan
>
>1. **Align on the Exemplar Pod Shape:** Finalize the proposed shape outlined above as the target baseline envelope to ensure realistic size overhead and API usage.
>2. **Document and Enforce:** Add this defined shape envelope to [sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md) to formally guarantee its scalability.
>3. **Fuzzing & Investigation:** Conduct fuzzing on other pod fields to identify any remaining areas with non-linear performance impacts.
>4. **Benchmark Updates:** Update upstream K8s tests and benchmarks to reflect these real-world findings, prioritizing benchmarks for the ManagedFields interning strategy and response compression bottlenecks.
>
>/sig scalability /sig api-machinery
>/cc @wojtek-t @mborsz @liggitt

Part of the shape of an object is the complexity of its field management, eg how many fields are jointly managed, number of field managers in use, etc.

Worth explicitly considering?

> Part of the shape of an object is the complexity of its field management, eg how many fields are jointly managed, number of field managers in use, etc.
> 
> Worth explicitly considering?

Maybe as internal metric, but for users this might be too ambiguous. We should use metrics that users can easily understand and can be documented. Also size of field identificator matters as much as it's used for referencing. Not only how fields are named in Pod spec, but also names assigned by users like pod name.

For the fuzzing/investigation step, would it be useful to treat Pod Shape as a small response-surface experiment rather than changing one field at a time?

The result here already shows why: two pods can have roughly the same serialized size while producing very different numbers of writes and very different control-plane cost.

A small first experiment could vary user-visible factors such as:

- labels / annotations
- regular container count
- init container count
- volume count
- env entry count
- readiness gates

while keeping the final serialized Pod size approximately fixed by adjusting an otherwise inert payload.

Instead of exhaustively testing every combination, we could use a small fractional-factorial or Latin-hypercube style sample and record the existing scalability outputs: API-server CPU/allocation, lifecycle write count, watch/event volume, scheduler/KCM memory, and scheduling tail latency.

The main thing I'd want to recover is not just the cost of each field independently, but interaction effects. For example, two individually cheap shape changes may become expensive together even though total Pod bytes stay constant.

This seems complementary to #142223/#142228: Pod shape changes how much work a nominally similar write causes, while those issues are measuring and reducing that write-path amplification. A fixed-size shape matrix could therefore become another input dimension for validating those optimizations, instead of benchmarking only one exemplar Pod.

This could start very small, perhaps 8-16 deliberately selected shapes around the current exemplar, and only expand if the response surface shows interesting nonlinearities.

If that fits the intended "Fuzzing & Investigation" work here, I'd be interested in prototyping the shape generator/reporting in perf-tests rather than changing the exemplar itself first.
